name: Global Team
tagline: Lead across cultures without losing anyone
about: Global Team helps leaders of multicultural, distributed teams run meetings everyone can speak in, plan around every location's holidays, adapt feedback across cultures, read indirect answers and repair misunderstandings before they harden.
persona: You are a seasoned leader of distributed global teams and a cross-cultural communication coach: practical, careful never to stereotype individuals, and focused on explicit norms over guesswork.

onboarding.title: One team, many cultures
onboarding.subtitle: Tell us where your people are and how you work; every plan uses it.
bullets: Meetings every culture can speak in

profile.label: Where your team is
profile.placeholder: London ×3, Bangalore ×4, São Paulo ×2, me in Berlin

profile.label: Current norms
profile.placeholder: weekly sync on video, Slack, English as working language

tools.title: Run a mixed-culture meeting
tools.subtitle: So the quiet half of the room speaks

inputs.label: Meeting and its purpose
inputs.placeholder: monthly planning; pick next quarter's priorities

inputs.label: The mix
options: Mostly one culture plus a few others

tools.prompt: Design a meeting for {people} people, mix: {mix}, purpose: {purpose}, across the profile's locations. Sections: steps as an agenda that engineers airtime (pre-read sent 24 hours ahead, a silent written round before discussion, invitation by name in a stated order, the most senior person speaking last); a table (Participation barrier — hierarchy / language / face / turn-taking norm | What you'll see | Fix in the moment); a quote with the opening 45 seconds that states the norms out loud; and a callout on facilitator mistakes such as cold-calling someone in front of their boss or treating silence as agreement.

tools.title: Holiday clash check
tools.subtitle: Observances in every location vs your deadlines

inputs.label: Deadlines and key meetings
inputs.placeholder: release 12 Oct; planning offsite 3–4 Nov; board pack due 20 Dec

tools.prompt: For the profile's locations, list the public holidays and major religious or cultural observances in the next {months}, and check them against these deadlines (if none are given, flag the busiest weeks instead): {deadlines}. Sections: a table (Observance | Location(s) | Dates (approx.) | Effect — office closed / many away / avoid scheduling); bullets naming each deadline or meeting at risk and the specific adjustment; a callout stating that dates for lunar and regional observances vary by year and region and must be confirmed with local team members; and a quote with a short message asking each location to confirm its dates.

tools.title: Feedback across cultures
tools.subtitle: Same message, adapted delivery

inputs.label: The feedback you need to give
inputs.placeholder: their status reports are late and too vague

inputs.label: To whom, where they're based
inputs.placeholder: engineer based in Tokyo, 2 years in the company

tools.prompt: Adapt this feedback for {to}, given the giver's style is '{your_style}': {message}. Sections: text on what is generally known about directness, hierarchy and face in that context, stated as tendencies not rules, with a warning against assuming the individual fits them; a quote with the adapted delivery (what to say, what to ask, how to check understanding); a table (Signal you might get | What it may mean | What to do); and a callout on the two mistakes each style makes with the other.

tools.title: Is that a yes or a no?
tools.subtitle: Read an indirect answer without guessing

inputs.label: What they said or wrote
inputs.placeholder: 'That might be a little difficult, but we will try our best.'

inputs.label: Who and their context
inputs.placeholder: vendor lead in Seoul, in a group email with their boss cc'd

tools.prompt: Decode this message from {who}: {words}. Sections: text with the likely literal meaning and two alternative readings, weighted; a table (Reading | Likelihood | Evidence in the text); a quote with a reply that checks the meaning without causing loss of face; and a callout on why to verify in a private channel rather than in the group.

tools.title: Repair a misunderstanding
tools.subtitle: Something landed badly across the divide

inputs.label: What happened
inputs.placeholder: I joked about deadlines in the all-hands; the Bangalore team went silent and one person asked to speak to HR

inputs.label: Who was hurt
options: Two team members with each other

tools.prompt: Repair this cross-cultural misunderstanding: {what}. Hurt party: {side}. Sections: text naming what probably happened on both sides without assigning blame; steps for the repair in order (private first, then public if needed, then a norm change); a quote with the apology or acknowledgement wording; a checklist of team norms to make explicit afterwards; and a callout on when this needs HR rather than a leader's repair.

disclaimer: Cultural notes describe general tendencies, not rules about individuals; when in doubt, ask the person.
